Mr. Speaker, during a recent Interparliamentary Union trip to Cyprus, the Canadian delegation had the opportunity to visit the Canadian peacekeeping contingent on that divided island.
The commanding officer of the whole UN peacekeeping force is the highly-regarded Canadian, General Milner. The 575-man Canadian contingent is made up primarily of the Princess Patricia Regiment, with some reservists as supplementals.
Everywhere we went on the island the Canadian forces were praised for their competence, fairness and co-operation, as well as for the excellent humanitarian work they are doing with both Greek and Turkish civilian populations.
We as Canadians can be very proud of our troops in Cyprus as an example of international peacekeeping at its best. We wish General Milner, Colonel Sutherland and the troops good health, safety and a successful mission.

Mr. Speaker, Canada has among other countries a reputation for tolerance and freedom.
Our country has been considerably enriched by the contributions of hundreds of thousands of immigrants. Among these immigrants, thousands of Armenians have found refuge in this country. Their dedication and unwavering loyalty have enriched the Canadian mosaic. The Armenian community's contribution to Canadian life is reflected in the churches, schools and cultural centres it has built across this country. In addition, they have made a major contribution to the arts, architecture, literature, photography, business, industry, law, public administration and education.

April 25, 1990
Yesterday was a memorable day for all our fellow citizens of Armenian origin, and especially in the riding of Ahuntsic.
Mr. Speaker, with Canadians across this country I want to say that the terrible events of the past of this valiant and courageous people must not be forgotten.

Mr. Speaker, the federal government is abandoning its moral and legal authority to lead the country on social policy; and it is forcing provinces to go it alone. This will result in greater regional inequality.
For example, the reaction from B.C. to the cap on the Canada Assistance Program has been to have the Public Gaming Branch speculate that the government controlled slot machines could raise as much as $120 million a year-enough to offset the loss of federal transfer payments.
The Socreds have even gone so far as to consider putting its own cap on, a cap on the amounts of money now earned by non-profit organizations that use casinos and bingos for raising money.
The Ontario Liberal government has reacted in its budget to the Tories' abandoned leadership by making it clear it cannot and will not revamp its welfare system as planned.
In addition, the Liberals in Ontario will be putting more emphasis on a shift to user-pay programming.
The mean-spirited Tory agenda is not an attack on the deficit, but an attack on the poor.

Mr. Speaker, I must strongly denounce the unworthy accusations and attitude of the member for York South-Weston, who called those who favour sovereignty for Quebec traitors and racists.
Should the hon. member for York South-Weston not have made the same remarks about those who, like APEC, promote a unilingual English Canada, or the hold-out premiers whose attitudes will lead to the weakening or disappearance of Canada in the Meech Lake affair?
The Liberal member for York South-Weston should have understood and recognized that Quebec separatists used to be great Canadians, until they were deprived of their rights, of a bilingual Canada and a strong Quebec.
In short, this Liberal member should have foreseen the dramatic effects his statements would have on all the other Quebecers who had until then been seeking a new Canada but who can no longer believe in it. Alas, this Chretien hack has sabotaged his own country which he claims to be virtuously defending!
Who is the real traitor, Mr. Speaker?

Mr. Speaker, I rise today to congratulate the citizens of Moncton as the city celebrates its 100th birthday as a city.
The city was granted its Charter on April 23, 1890. April 23, 1990 was a special day-from the Citizenship Court swearing in of new Canadians, followed by students participating in the historical review "One Hundred Steps", to later in the day when Moncton City Council and Premier Frank McKenna went through a light-hearted re-enactment of the original granting of the Charter.
Moncton certainly lived up to its unofficial motto: "The City to Watch".

The history of Moncton is very varied. We have had shipbuilding, railways and now high technology. Our city is solidly built on two cultures. We are a microcosm of Canada.

My father and I both were mayors of the city of Moncton and, as all Monctonians, proud of its accomplishments. Happy Birthday, Moncton.

April 25, 1990



50TH ANNIVERSARY OF WOMEN'S RIGHT TO VOTE IN QUEBEC

In a show of solidarity with all women in Quebec, Mr. Speaker, I want to point out that today marks the 50th anniversary of their right to vote in provincial elections.
It was after constant and unrelenting struggles that, on April 25, 1940, pioneers like Marie Gerin-Lajoie, Therese Casgrain and Idola St-Jean were successful in having the Quebec legislature acknowledge their right to equality in chosing their elected representatives, men or women.
In difficult times, these women paved the way for what has now become an irreversible movement towards full equality. Today's feminists owe them a lot.

Mr. Speaker, pursuant to their service reliability program, Canada Post management made a public commitment in 1987 that they would guarantee regular delivery of standard letters properly addressed between major urban centres within the following time frames: two working days for letters sent within the same urban centre; three working days for letters to another major urban centre in the same province; and four working days to a major urban centre in another province.
The Ernst and Young report tabled yesterday and based on a survey of more than 50,000 items mailed during the first three months of the year indicates a service performance averaging 97 per cent of set objectives. Specifically, the Sherbrooke and Quebec City regions recorded 99 per cent, Montreal, Laval and Longueuil 98 per cent, and Winnipeg, Regina and Saskatoon 99 per cent.
Mr. Speaker, Canada Post and all its employees are to be commended for their outstanding service to the Canadian people.
Hurrah for Canada Post!

Mr. Speaker, with the advent of the spring lobster fishery in Nova Scotia, lobster fishermen in Nova Scotia and in the Gulf are nervous about their chances to survive another year.
As a result of lobster size regulations recently enacted by the United States Congress, prices have plummeted, falling to $2.50 a pound in southern Nova Scotia, well below last year's price of $4.50. Some industry observers think Gulf prices may soon fall below $2.
Yesterday's leak of the preliminary judgment by the binational free trade panel looking into the size regulations will no doubt put even more downward pressure on prices at the start of the season.
This is potentially disastrous. It will cost lobster fishermen untold thousands of dollars in lost income, maybe even their livelihood.
Atlantic Canadians cannot afford a crisis in yet another sector of the fishery. I call on the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans to provide immediate help, both to cushion these fishermen against the offending size regulations and to help them find alternative markets for these lobsters.

I think it is absurd that, at a time when tens of thousands of unemployed workers cannot find jobs, so many employers are complaining about a shortage of qualified manpower.

speakeroldname: Hon. Herb Gray (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have a question for the Minister of Finance.
Today, the Canadian Real Estate Association announced that last month the sales of existing homes and condominiums in major cities dropped by 22 per cent compared to March of last year.
Speaking about this, Carl Beigie, a leading Canadian economist, said:
We haven't seen the worst of it yet. It's like a house of cards. We're just starting to see the start of a really bad financial problem.
So I ask the minister this. Why are he and his government insisting on pursuing economic policies that are creating the start of a bad financial problem? Why is he doing this to Canadians, Canadian families, and Canadian workers?

Mr. Speaker, I have responded to questions along those lines before. Perhaps I could read from an editorial which appeared in The Financial Post today.
It's just as well the governor can weather the criticism; if he heeded his critics and loosened the monetary floodgates, we would really be in a pickle.
The editorial goes on to state:
- inflationary pressures have been stronger in Canada than in the U.S-But if our costs are not contained, how can we remain competitive? Easy money and a lower Canadian dollar may deliver a temporary advantage-Any weakening of the Bank's resolve to maintain the value of the currency will be quickly pounced upon by long-term investors who will demand an inflation premium-Once such a flight begins, it's hard to stop.
These comments in this editorial from The Financial Post set out quite clearly the problem that we face as a country, that we are Committed to dealing with, and that we find absolutely necessary to deal with and not to run
away from, as did my hon. friend opposite in the late 1970s and the early 1980s.

speakeroldname: Hon. Herb Gray (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I, too, have a quote that I consider credible, and so will Canadians because it is from President Maurice R. Faraggi of the Canadian Real Estate Association. He said that the Canadian Real Estate Association:
-believes there is room for interest rates to come down and in fact called upon the Central Bank to reduce them. Instead we see increase after increase, putting enormous pressure on Canadian consumers and impeding the government's own deficit reduction goals by increasing the cost of servicing its enormous debt. Enough is enough. Interest rates must come down!
So says Maurice Faraggi, the head of a major business organization, the Canadian Real Estate Association.
If the minister is so concerned about inflation, then why is it that senior officials of the Prime Minister's own office and the Bank of Canada have been given pay increases of up to 17.6 per cent? Over the same period working people have received increases of only some 12.9 per cent? Why is the minister asking Canadians to bite the bullet on cost-of-living increases when he is not doing the same thing for the staff of the Prime Minister's office and the Bank of Canada?
Mr. Speaker, I am glad that the hon. member has asked those questions because I want to put the accurate picture on the record.
Oh, oh!

As far as the staff of the Prime Minister's office is concerned, the article is wrong. Until this month, the staff had not received an increase since the last election-since the last election. The staff received a 4.2 per cent increase this month which is not retroactive. That is one raise of 4.2 per cent in nearly two years. That is not excessive.
As far as the Bank of Canada is concerned, according to the article that I saw in the newspaper, the bank's salaiy structure in the 1987 to 1989 period was up 12.6 per cent. The public sector settlements during that same period were 14 per cent. Private sector settlements during that same period were 14.8 per cent. The Bank of Canada is in line with what is happening in terms of
April 25, 1990

Oral Questions
settlements in other parts of the public sector, as well as in the private sector.
I might point out that personal disposable income per capita during that 1987 to 1989 period is up 25.2 per cent.

speakeroldname: Hon. Herb Gray (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Minister of Finance avoided any comments on the salary increase of the Governor of the Bank of Canada which, according to my information, is above the level he mentioned.
I also want to ask the Minister of Finance why he did not react to what was said by the President of the Canadian Real Estate Association, who asked him for major reductions in interest rates. Why is the minister so reluctant to respond to one of our country's important businessmen?

Mr. Speaker, I do not know how the Leader of the Opposition can say I have not given an answer to the question that he says was asked by the Canadian Real Estate Association. I answered that question on Monday. I answered it yesterday. I answered it again today. If he would like me to repeat it again, I will give him the answer.
First, let me say that I am not happy about interest rates being where they are today. I would like to see interest rates lower. It would certainly make my job a lot easier as Minister of Finance.
I do know that if we let these inflationary pressures get out of hand we will be back to where we started at around a 5.5 per cent inflation rate in the mid-1970s. It moved up to 13 per cent because the government of the day did not take the problem seriously. We are taking the problem seriously. We are trying to head off the problem before it gets out of control and before it leads to a 13 per cent inflation rate and the 20 per cent to 25 per cent interest rates that we saw in the early 1980s.
Surely my hon. friend's memory is not that bad that he cannot remember the damage that that period did to the economy of Canada. We are trying to avoid that with the policies we are following.

Mr. Speaker, in his Budget the Minister of Finance explained that the average interest rate in Canada this year should be around 11.1 per cent. Subsequently, the Prime Minister of Canada told us that interest rates should go down very shortly.
Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of Finance. Does the government set monetary policy for this country or does the Financial Post, which is the impression we get from his answer to the Leader of the Liberal Party?
Mr. Speaker, first, let me congratulate my hon. friend for having been moved from the back row up to the second row. I would caution him not to be too influenced by those people on his left flank.
Flear, hear!
I might also say that he should be pretty cautious about the ideas he takes from his right flank as well.
Oh, oh!

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: Perhaps the minister could respond to the question.

Mr. Speaker, these are serious matters. I have discussed them at some length in the House during the past two days, and I am willing to do so again. I am willing to discuss these matters further at committee, if members wish me to do so.
I reported what was stated in The Financial Post. That is a responsible newspaper expressing, I think, a point of view that is a responsible point of view. It is a point of view that I think is important for Canadians to understand.
As I have indicated, I am not happy about high interest rates. I would like to see them come down. But I want to see them come down on a permanent basis, not on a short-term basis to then find that interest rates and inflation are much higher. The problem would be much more difficult to resolve at that stage, as we found out in 1980 to 1982 when we went through a very serious recession and we saw all the damage that caused.

April 25, 1990
Oral Questions

Mr. Speaker, I have a supplementary question for the Minister of Finance.
For months, if not for the last couple of years, the Governor of the Bank of Canada has said that inflation is public enemy number one. Does the Minister of Finance not believe that the time has come to recognize that the high interest rate policy and the high value of the Canadian dollar are creating the real public enemy number one in this country, which is a recession? Does the minister not realize that this is what the end result of his policies will be? As a result, will he change those policies?

Mr. Speaker, if we could go back and look at every recession that has happened, at least since the war, we would see that there has always been a period of high inflation, inflation that got out of control, before we had a recession. What we are trying to do is to keep the level of inflation down, avoid the problems that a high level of inflation causes, along with the blow-off that comes from it and the sudden drop that follows. That is the essence of the policies we are following.
My hon. friend says that there is a lot of advice to the contrary. I understand that. But I can take my hon. friend back to August of 1988 and August of 1989 when we had the unanimous recommendation from the provincial premiers to reduce interest rates. If we had reduced interest rates at that time, we would have considerably higher levels of inflation today and we would be that much closer to a serious recession of the type my friend is talking about, the type of recession we are committed to avoid.

Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Deputy Prime Minister.
In July, 1988, the Prime Minister told a meeting in Toronto: "We will implement and build on our national child care program". During the last election campaign in October, 1988, the Prime Minister said again of the government's child care legislation: "We will be reintroducing that legislation and pass it as soon as Parliament comes back after the election".
Parliament has been back for a year and half, and we are still waiting for child care legislation. I ask the Deputy Prime Minister this. Will the government make a commitment now to bring in child care legislation this year?

speakeroldname: Hon. Marcel Danis (Minister of State (Youth) and Minister of State (Fitness and Amateur Sport) and Deputy Leader of the Government in the House of Commons):
speakerposition: Minister of State (Fitness and Amateur Sport); Minister of State (Youth); Deputy Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party Deputy House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as the Minister of National Health and Welfare said yesterday, and as was announced in the Speech from the Throne on April 3,1989, this government will have a child care program implemented before 1993.
If it had not been for the other place, we would now have a child care program implemented.

My supplementary question is directed to the Deputy Prime Minister, Mr. Speaker.
There are 1.3 million children in Canada in need of child care spaces. There are just over 200,000 licensed child care spaces. Now the government is saying to wait until 1993.

Mr. Speaker, in 1984 during the election campaign, the Prime Minister promised to improve child care services. Six years later, the situation is still the same. A whole generation has grown up since. Will this government take action now instead of waiting until the next election campaign?

speakeroldname: Hon. Marcel Danis (Minister of State (Youth), Minister of State (Fitness and Amateur Sport) and Deputy Leader of the Government in the House of Commons):
speakerposition: Minister of State (Fitness and Amateur Sport); Minister of State (Youth); Deputy Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party Deputy House Leader
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, when the Leader of the New Democratic Party says that in 1984 we talked about this program, she is right. However, we not only talked about it, we passed legislation in the House of Commons. It has not been implemented, not through the fault of the government but of the other place. The Senate failed to pass legislation, not us. We did our job, and the Leader of the NDP should congratulate the government on the good work it did during its first term.

The government knows that that legislation was not put in force because it was unacceptable to every child care group in this country.
The government continually refuses to live up to its commitments to the children of this country and is abandoning the families of this country. The government has promised that child care facilities will be available in all new and renovated federal government buildings. Yet the government is breaking its promise again for new federal buildings. I cite one example in Whitehorse, Yukon.
Will this government guarantee now that child care facilities, as it has been agreed to with the Public Service Commission in Whitehorse, Yukon, and throughout Canada, will be assured in all federal buildings?

speakeroldname: Hon. Marcel Danis (Minister of State (Youth) and Minister of State (Fitness and Amateur Sport) and Deputy Leader of the Government in the House of Commons):
speakerposition: Minister of State (Fitness and Amateur Sport); Minister of State (Youth); Deputy Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party Deputy House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. leader of the New Democratic Party says that we did nothing. We put $6.4 billion for child care programs in our last mandate. How can the hon. member say that was nothing; $6.4 billion.
The only reason it is not implemented is because the other place would not do so. It is not the fault of this government, it is the fault of the other place. Maybe the Liberals should talk to their colleagues in the other place.

Mr. Speaker, in the absence of the Minister of National Health and Welfare, my question is directed to the Deputy Prime Minister. Currently there are more than 2 million children under age 12 who require day care. Yet, thanks to this government's previous commitment to day care, there are only enough licensed spaces for about 10 per cent of these children.
My question is, quite simply, when is this government going to recognize the day care crisis in Canada and give us a firm date on when the new legislation will be introduced? Nineteen ninety-three is not acceptable.

speakeroldname: Hon. Marcel Danis (Minister of State (Youth) and Minister of State (Fitness and Amateur Sport) and Deputy Leader of the Government in the House of Commons):
speakerposition: Minister of State (Fitness and Amateur Sport); Minister of State (Youth); Deputy Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party Deputy House Leader

Mr. Speaker, 1993 may not be acceptable to
Oral Questions
the hon. member, but 1988 would have been acceptable to this government when it passed the legislation.
I am surprised that this question would come from a member of the Official Opposition. All the member would have had to do was talk to the members of the Liberal Party in the other place and we would now have a child care program in place in Canada.

Mr. Speaker, the member should refrain from giving the government's old refrain and answer the chorus of discontent in this country. Working mothers are not among the 15 per cent of Canadians who still support this government.
If and when the government decides to live up to its new-found interest in children, is this government prepared to guarantee to this House that new legislation will not put a funding cap on new spaces, will set all-important national standards for high quality care and assure Canadians for the first time that it will provide for the national enforcement of those standards?

speakeroldname: Hon. Marcel Danis (Minister of State (Youth), Minister of State (Fitness and Amateur Sport) and Deputy Leader of the Government in the House of Commons):
speakerposition: Minister of State (Fitness and Amateur Sport); Minister of State (Youth); Deputy Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party Deputy House Leader
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, for the second time, I am surprised to have a question on a national child care program from a Liberal member of the Official Opposition. This government passed legislation that created a national child care program and allocated $6.4 billion to it. The only reason many children in this country do not have a national day care system is the Senate, the other place.
Everyone in Canada opposed your proposal.

speakerposition: Minister of State (Fitness and Amateur Sport); Minister of State (Youth); Deputy Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party Deputy House Leader
speechtext: And I hope that the Liberal member opposite will give the Senate the message about child care, and about the unemployment insurance bill as well.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Liberal Party House Leader; Liberal Party Deputy House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question was for the Secretary of State, but in his absence, I shall direct it to the Deputy Prime Minister.

April 25, 1990
Oral Questions
Yesterday, the Secretary of State told us in this House that he had called Saskatchewan Education Minister Meiklejohn and obtained an assurance from him that his government intended to move quickly on implementing a school system controlled and run by the minority.
Mr. Speaker, today's Le Devoir informs us that the same education minister said that he was not sure he could proceed with this program of minority-controlled schools promised by the Saskatchewan government.
I ask the minister to obtain a firm commitment in writing from the Saskatchewan government that it will keep its promise to its minority and provide Saskatchewan francophones with a school system that meets their needs and which they will manage and control, in a clearly specified time frame.

speakeroldname: Hon. Lucien Bouchard (Minister of the Environment):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, Prime Minister Mulroney wrote to the Saskatchewan government very recently to deeply deplore the delay in setting up the separately managed school system. He even offered the Saskatchewan government legal services and the federal government's legal expertise, since the Saskatchewan government used this argument to justify the delay in establishing the new system.
The National Commission of Francophone Parents today issued a press release congratulating Prime Minister Mulroney for his leadership on this issue.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Liberal Party House Leader; Liberal Party Deputy House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the minister may satisfy himself with a letter from the Prime Minister, but that does not give that minority anything in terms of concrete actions from its provincial government. An agreement was signed in 1988 for $26 million over 10 years to provide for a service, the implementation of a system of control and management of the schools by the minority.
Will the minister give this House his assurance that within that bilateral federal-provincial agreement no moneys will be spent at this time until a reasonable, acceptable, concrete commitment by the province has been given to the francophone population of that province that meets with their ideas of what should be in place in Saskatchewan?

speakeroldname: Hon. Lucien Bouchard (Minister of the Environment):
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, nobody can raise any question on the sincerity of the efforts made by this government to promote French outside of Quebec. I would remind my hon. colleagues from the other side of the House that today the Fransaskais themselves have issued a communique recognizing the leadership shown by the Prime Minister on this issue.

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Finance and concerns high interest rates and inflation. Over the last year increases in interest rates have meant that monthly mortgage payments on an average home have increased by over $200 per month. Because of taxes and payroll deductions, in order to have $200 a month a person must earn $400 a month. This is a major cause of wage pressure and wage inflation.
In the face of this clear evidence, will the minister now admit that high interest rates are a prime cause of inflation, not a cure for inflation?

No, I do
not accept that statement at all, Mr. Speaker. Let me take my friend back to what has happened during the course of 1989.
We had bank credit, that is loan demand for business loans, for consumer loans, for household mortgage loans, all growing in excess of 10 per cent per annum throughout this period and for mortgage loans the rate of growth ranged between 15 and 20 per cent per annum.
If we had reduced interest rates at that time, as my colleague has said that he would like us to have done, we would increase the demand for those loans. That loan demand would have been much higher than it was and that just sows the seeds for future inflation.
This is precisely what we are trying to avoid. High interest rates are the symptom of the problem. The cause of the problem is inflation. Inflation causes high interest rates.

Mr. Speaker, my supplementary question is for the Minister of Finance. It is obvious that the government does not care about child care but it also becoming apparent that it does not care about homeless children.
April 25, 1990

Each increase of 1 per cent in the mortgage rates means another 100,000 Canadians cannot afford to purchase a home. Housing resales have plummeted. Houses starts will fall within six months.
The Minister of Finance knows that housing construction is one of the main engines of our economy. Will the minister now say that interest rates have peaked, or will he continue with his bull-headed high interest rate policy and force this country into a full recession?

Mr. Speaker, housing starts, according to the most recent figures, I believe, were 222,000 on an annual basis. They have been in excess of 200,000 starts a year for three or four years now. So we have had a very strong housing market that has been well supported by the policies that have been followed by this government. That is one of the reasons why we have unemployment down to the lowest levels that it has been for many, many years now. This suggests to me that our economy is operating at high levels of activity which is leading to the levels of inflationary pressures that we are seeing today.
But, Mr. Speaker, my colleague is forgetting that in the 1970s and early 1980s, when problems of inflation were ignored or were not taken seriously enough by the previous government, we ended up with exactly the problem that my hon. friend tells me that we should be trying to avoid.
That is why we are doing what we are doing, to stop the inflationary pressures where they are now, to start the levels of inflation turning down rather than continuing up, because if they do continue up, we will most certainly see the problems of high interest rates, high unemployment and a plummet in housing starts which my hon. friend is concerned about.

Mr. Speaker, I have a question for the Minister of State (Employment and Immigration). Some 54 weeks have elapsed since this Government tabled in this House the Labour Force Development Strategy. Also, Bill C-21 has been passed by this House.
Oral Questions
Right now, Mr. Speaker, a number of my constituents have to wait between 14 and 20 weeks to be entitled to UI benefits. I would like to know from the Minister what she intends to do to help the unemployed in my constituency, because they are hurting.

speakeroldname: Hon. Monique Vezina (Minister of State (Employment and Immigration) and Minister of State (Seniors)):
speakerposition: Minister of State (Seniors); Minister of State (Employment and Immigration)
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member is expressing the concerns of many Canadian workers. I would like first to reassure this House and express this Government's intention to provide Canadian workers with a long-term economic future.
This being said, we all know that Bill C-21 is based on a variable entrance requirement which will provide us with a system that is fairer. Under that requirement, workers in high unemployment areas will only need 10 weeks of employment. The requirement becomes higher in more prosperous areas. It may be important to add that there will no longer be that six week penalty for seasonal workers who apply for benefits more than once during one year.
I would like to take this opportunity to once more urge the other House to pass within the shortest possible time frame Bill C-21, which will be of help to our workers.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: I wish to draw to members' attention the presence in the gallery of the United Kingdom Select Committee on Members' Interests, led by Sir Geoffrey Johnson Smith.
Hear, hear!

Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Acting Minister of Justice or perhaps the Leader of the Government in the House of Commons.
When the Minister of Justice visited the Ecole Polytechnique in Montreal recently, students presented the minister with 25 boxes of petitions, with more than
500,000	signatures, asking for more effective control of firearms. On that occasion, the minister promised to table a bill in the House by the end of this month. Since

April 25, 1990
Oral Questions
it is now April 25, could the minister inform the House when we will have this bill before the House? On what date?

I want to thank my hon. friend for the question. It is, indeed, a very serious situation. The government has been reviewing the present firearms legislation for some time now. I can assure my friend that it was a very extensive consultation process because in my former capacity I was heavily involved in that consultation process.
The new minister is seized of the matter, and I am sure that she will be bringing it forward as soon as she has an opportunity to familiarize herself with the legislation and with all the ramifications.

Mr. Speaker, the minister promised to bring in that bill before the end of the month.
Can the minister tell this House whether the law will ban the sale of military and paramilitary weapons to private citizens?
I want to remind the minister that the gun that was used to kill those 14 women at the University of Montreal was a Ruger semi-automatic rifle which could fire up to 50 rounds of ammunition and which is now used by several police SWAT squads and military forces.
Does the minister and the government think that this is the type of gun that should be sold to private citizens over the counter?

Mr. Speaker, I should advise my hon. friend that the initiative started off to look at banning the sale of automatic weapons which had been converted to semi-automatic weapons for the purpose of bringing them into the country. Since this legislation had not been revised for some ten years, there was an effort made to review all of the ramifications of the firearms control legislation in an effort to improve it.
I can assure my hon. friend that we take the sale of military weapons very, very seriously. My colleague, the Minister of Justice, is looking at the question of magazine size, but there is no intention to ban semi-automatic weapons.

speakeroldname: Mr. Francis G. LeBlanc (Cape Breton Highlands - Canso):
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Secretary of State for External Affairs. There are reports today that the Free Trade Panel is about to support the U.S. measure to restrict exports of Canadian lobster to the United States. Considering the devastating impact of such a decision, what does the minister intend to do to remove the uncertainty this U.S. measure has created in the lobster industry in the Maritimes, at a time when the fishing season is about to begin?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. Joe Clark (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the House will remember that on December 21, Canada invoked Chapter 18 dispute resolution mechanisms of the free trade agreement to have a bi-national panel set up that would challenge American amendments to the Magnuson Act, amendments which would effectively prohibit the importation into the United States of live lobster smaller than the American minimum size. That panel has completed its interim report. That was a confidential report until elements of it were published today in the press.
As the member will know, there is a procedure which allows the Government of Canada and the affected industry to comment on this interim report up until April 30. There were consultations held yesterday in Halifax with regard to the comments that Canada would make. Those comments will be made prior to April 30.
I remind the House that the final report does not come in until May 15. We intend to continue to press the interests of Canadian lobster fishermen.
Mr. Francis G. LeBlanc (Cape Breton Highlands-
Canso): Mr. Speaker, last fall when the U.S. legislation the minister is talking about was introduced, the Prime Minister promised to use the full weight of government influence to prevent it from being passed. Yet it was passed and now we have reports that this measure, which the Minister for International Trade has called "a trade
April 25, 1990

distorting measure", has been found acceptable by the bi-national panel.
Will the minister tell this House today what further action he will take to lift the cloud which this U.S. trade restriction has created on the Atlantic lobster industry?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. Joe Clark (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Prime Minister said that he would bring the full weight of Canadian influence to bear. I was with him when he raised the matter specifically with the President of the United States and argued strongly that the legislation not be proceeded with. Unfortunately, the President moved in his own jurisdiction to proceed with the amendments. We then immediately triggered the provisions that exist under the Canada-U.S. Free Trade Agreement.
A panel was established in accordance with the provisions of the FTA. The panel was not unanimous on the basic question that is of concern to Canada which is what we believe to be the trade distorting implications of the U.S. measure.
There has been an interim report. We are disappointed with the interim report. We are availing ourselves of the provisions set out in the FTA and will comment on the interim report with the hope that the final report which has yet to come will be more satisfactory from the Canadian perspective.

Mr. Speaker, I have a question for the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources. Two days ago, during the energy and transportation session of the parliamentary forum on global climate change, all three expert witnesses, including the President of the Canadian Automobile Association, condemned the government for going in the wrong direction by cutting funding for energy alternatives and conservation by over 90 per cent since 1984.
As it is a waste of time to consult further on what is universally agreed and as, in the words of the environment minister, "the price of inaction is too high", will
Oral Questions
the energy minister restore funding for these very effective programs to 1984 levels now, and not use the excuse of The Green Plan discussions to further stall what virtually everyone agrees should be done immediately?

I believe that money should be spent for further R and D so that we can get more energy efficiency, rather than pay for the salaries that were then in place.

However, given that Petro-Canada is well placed to take a leadership role in helping to make Canada, in the words of The Green Plan paper, "the industrial world's most environmentally friendly country", will the minister go back to his cabinet colleagues and urge them to scrap their plans to privatize Petro-Canada? Will he urge them to start using Canada's energy corporation actively and creatively to promote a more environmentally responsible energy future?

April 25, 1990

speakername: Mr. Walter Van  De Walle@St. Albert

speakeroldname: Right Hon. Joe Clark (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we are deeply concerned about the political situation and the abuse of human rights in Burma, which is now known as Myanmar. The government of that country has made it clear that it will not welcome political observers. Indeed, it has gone a step further and indicated that it is putting a severe limitation upon the visits by tourists and others to the country because it expects that some of those tourists, journalists or others, might function as election observers. I think that makes it extremely unlikely that the election that is planned for that country will be a democratic or a full election.
We are calling in the Ambassador of Myanmar to Canada to express our most serious objections to that procedure and we are making those representations in Myanmar itself.

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Solicitor General. Recent media reports have indicated that Correctional Service Canada plans to install a newly conceived and designed parole office in downtown Toronto. This office would exclusively serve a concentrated number of high risk offenders who are released on mandatory supervision. This particular office location is not far from where the Tema Conter tragedy took place a couple of years ago.
What steps is Correctional Service Canada taking to explain to the community what exactly is being planned here and why these so-called high risk offenders are being released in the first place to the community prior to the termination of their sentences?

speechtext:

With respect to the "super office" that he is referring to, there is a pilot project that will be under way and I am convinced that the service will do whatever consultation is necessary in order to make sure that everybody is aware of what is coming down.

In view of the fact that this type of initiative is a new concept for Correctional Service, specifically what steps are going to be taken by the government to increase the security and protection for the public and to reassure them that the correction system maintains public security as its primary goal?

subsubtopic: REMARKS OF HON. MEMBER FOR YORK SOUTH-WESTON
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I appreciate this opportunity to clarify the remarks I made at the Liberal leadership forum in Halifax on the weekend.
I would like to make it absolutely clear at the outset that it was not my intention in any way, shape, or form to insult Quebecers or anyone else. I did not in my statement use the words "sedition" or "treason", words that have been attributed to me. I did not cite the Criminal Code of Canada. Yet there are those, for political reasons I suspect, who have attributed certain words to me.
I did indicate in Halifax that in my view separatists were traitors. Those were the words I used. I was not referring to Quebecers. I was referring to the small

April 25, 1990
Privilege
minority of individuals who have as their raison d'etre the destruction of our country, who promote actively on an ongoing basis the division of Canada. I did not mean the word in the criminal sense. On the contrary, I meant it in the dictionary sense, if you will, and I would like to cite the Oxford dictionary definition of "traitor".
One who is false to his allegiance or acts disloyally (to country-
Mr. Speaker, after our election when we became members of Parliament, we were all required to swear an oath of allegiance before we could take our seats in this place. That is a requirement in law under the British North America Act. Each and every one of us in this House had to swear the following oath:
I, -, do swear, that I will be faithful and bear true allegiance to Her Majesty Queen Elizabeth the Second.
That is required under the British North America Act, The Fifth Schedule. Those who for religious reasons feel it necessary to affirm in lieu of the oath are required to state that:
I, -, do solemnly, sincerely and truly affirm and declare that taking of an oath is according to my religious belief unlawful, and I do also solemnly, sincerely and truly affirm and declare that I will be faithful and bear true allegiance to Her Majesty Queen Elizabeth the Second.
That is the duty and the responsibility of each and every one of us who has been elected to the Parliament of Canada.
With respect to separatists, there are a number of people who have different definitions or interpretations of the word "separatist" and who is a separatist and who is not, and whether a separatist is a nationalist, and whether a nationalist is a separatist. In the context of my comments at Halifax, I was referring to those who have as their preoccupation, their raison d'etre, the division of Canada. If that is their ambition and goal, then how can it be said, according to the dictionary definition, that the person is loyal to Canada.
In so far as the words "racist" and "bigot" are concerned, I did not call anyone a racist or a bigot. I did not refer to any particular individual as a racist or a bigot. I did not introduce the words racism and bigotry into this debate. A few months ago the Prime Minister said the following, and I agree with him with respect to this particular quote.
In the article entitled "Language Intolerance is Near Racism, PM", the Prime Minister said: "Great nations are built by generosity and understanding and by resisting the temptation to knock one's neighbours or diminish someone who is different. Once you get after language the next thing is race, the next thing is religion and the next thing is colour. That is the absence of tolerance."
The Prime Minister said on September 14, 1984, and I quote: "To try to curry the favour of the Parti Quebecois organization during a leadership campaign is dangerous to the candidate who does it. It is dangerous for the future of the party he seeks to lead and it is dangerous to the future of the united country he seeks to govern. You do not become Leader of the Progressive Conservative Party of Canada by playing footsie with the Parti Quebecois."
At the time, he was expressing concerns I have, that all too often, in recognizing the sensitivity of the matter, it appears difficult to stand up and fight for Canada, to defend Canada and to take to task those who have as their vocation the division of Canada. What I intended at Halifax was to take the separatists to task for their goal and ambition.
Others have used similar language. It is strong language, but we have the Charter of Rights and Freedoms in Canada. Each and every one of us is afforded certain rights and privileges, and one of them is freedom of speech. I do not deny those who advocate separatism the right, in a lawful manner, to advocate separatism or division. That is their right. As long as it is not done in a violent fashion or as long as one does not promote violence, it is their right. But it is also my right as a Canadian and as a member of Parliament to stand up and debate and discuss in a very firm fashion my views with respect to the issue of national unity.
A great number of members in this House have made comments as of late with respect to the whole question of the Meech Lake Accord or national unity. The member for Kitchener, for example, just a few weeks ago said and I quote:
When I listen to some of my Quebec colleagues I don't like what I am hearing. I sometimes wonder if it almost treason to keep talking about separatism.

I see an insult to Quebecers, I see a breach of the privileges of this House and I see a breach of our privileges in Quebec, because of the undue burden they would have us carry. Do not ask us to forget that we are Quebecers and that we come from a nation who has had to struggle relentlessly for its survival. A Quebecer coming to Ottawa must not forget that.
Coming to Ottawa, we also became aware of the risk we were taking. It has sometimes been called "le beau risque". It was a risk worth taking and, as far as I am concerned, it still is.

speakeroldname: Hon. Bill McKnight (Minister of National Defence):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise to extend on behalf of all members of this House our sympathy to Captain Hollis Tucker's family, following a CF-18 crash last Sunday on Vancouver Island.
I would also like to take this opportunity to extend our condolences, on behalf of the House, to Captain Kirk Leuty's family following a tragic CF-18 accident last week in Germany, and to say to their comrades that we understand their loss of good friends. We extend our sympathy to them.
As a result of these accidents, Mr. Speaker, you will recall that I ordered a 48-hour suspension of all CF-18
Routine Proceedings
operational training activity. At that time I said I would inform the House and my colleagues as to what had come about in that 48-hour time period.
This measure was to allow our senior Air Force commanders time to assess the situation and, during this period of time, do an intensive assessment by commanders at all levels of our fighter operations has been conducted.
Pursuant to this assessment and in the absence of an exact determination of the causes of recent accidents, the Air Commander has modified training materials and procedures, exercise scenarios, flight envelopes-for example, the altitude limitations, the air speed, and so on-to reinforce the safety aspects of the safety/realism equation.
Based on these changes, I have accepted the recommendation of my military commanders that the return to routine tasking and operation commence as air crew are briefed on these new measures. These briefings will conclude this week, and I expect that routine tasking will begin next week.

Madam Speaker, I join the Minister of National Defence, also on behalf of all members of this House, in extending our sympathy to the families of Captain Hollis Tucker and Captain Kirk Leuty, and indeed, to the families of all the CF-18 pilots who have lost their lives in the line of duty in the service of their country.
Our Canadian military won in war the reputation of being professional, a reputation that they fiercely protect and unquestionably maintain in peace. It is that reputation and a continuing trust in their professional conduct and judgment that allows this side of the House to appreciate the Defence Minister's statement.
That statement, as I understand it, is that, although an exact determination of the cause of recent accidents has not been found, with restrictions and appropriate briefings, including special emphasis on the safety/combat realism equation, routine taskings will begin next week. Nevertheless, I enjoin the minister to continue to pursue vigorously a "tiger-team" approach to finding the cause of these tragic accidents and to make the results public in a timely manner.
I think it is appropriate to inject a thought at this point in time. What a society gets from its armed forces is

April 25, 1990
Routine Proceedings
exactly what it asks for-nothing more and nothing less. What it asks for tends to be a reflection of what it is.
When a country looks at its fighting force and what it does, it is really looking into a mirror. If the mirror is a true one, the reflection it sees there will be its own. It is within the context of this principle, and without prejudice to the follow-on investigations that may follow or any other further restrictions that may be placed on the CF-18 aircraft, that guides our response to this very sensitive and important issue.

Madam Speaker, I, too, on behalf of my party and all members of the House, wish to extend our sincerest condolences to the families of Captain Hollis Tucker and Captain Kirk Leuty. It is very sad and tragic that in training, whether it be the the Air Command, Army or Maritime Command, from time to time there are casualties, some of them the extreme casualty of death.
However, we do have a responsibility in this Chamber to make absolutely certain that everything is done to minimize those tragic incidents. I commend the minister for his 48-hour moratorium. I do question, however, whether in 48 hours enough information could be obtained to permit him, not to lift the moratorium, but at least to allow routine flying to recommence with that particular airplane. However, he has information from his senior officers and staff. Obviously, he is satisfied at this point that routine training flights will not jeopardize the lives of those other pilots who are flying. I would, however, stress that there is always an element of danger, particularly in such a sophisticated plane as the CF-18.
What I would like to see is a full, public inquiry. We live in an age of information; we are an informational society. People want to know, people have the right to know, and if I can sound crass for a moment, the taxpayers of Canada have a lot of money invested in the Canadian Armed Forces and indeed in those planes that are in the range of $35 million to $37 million each.
I am getting a little tired of the in-house, behind closed doors approach that National Defence usually adopts in its investigations. That is appropriate in wartime or if national security is at stake. However, if it is purely a safety measure, an investigation should be established so that all interested persons, either military
or non-military, have an opportunity to find all the facts and all the information as they were presented.
Finally, I find it difficult to accept that the CF-18s should continue to practice low-level tactical flying exercises related to such things as the follow-on force attack and the pursuit of cruise missiles at a time when we are making every effort to wind down what used to be called the cold war. By "we" I mean our country, the United States, certainly Europe, and the Eastern Bloc. I see no practical purposes served in those particular simulated low-level tactical flights in view of the high risk involved in terms of lives being lost at this time.
I hope that the minister will see fit to open up the inquiry somewhere down the road in the not too distant future so that we all may benefit from the information and the input that goes into that inquiry.

speechtext: I wish to inform the House that by reason of the statement by minister, Government Orders will be extended by nine minutes.

The House resume from Tuesday, April 24, consideration of the motion of Mr. Wilson (Etobicoke-Centre): That Bill C-69, an Act to amend certain statutes to enable restraint of government expenditures, be now read a second time and refer to a legislative committee; and the amendment of Ms. Langan.

Madam Speaker, today I rise to take part in the debate on Bill C-69. This legislation covers many areas and it will have a very negative effect on the province of Prince Edward Island, especially with the transfer payments. The freezing of transfer payments means that Prince Edward Island will lose about $13 million over the next two years. That is the money that is given to the provinces to help education and health.
However, today I am here to discuss and debate Bill C-69, as the party critic for Energy, Mines and Resources. This legislation, among other things, eliminates the Canadian Exploration Incentive Program, known as CEIP. The CEIP issue combines two issues that are very
April 25, 1990

important to me: mining policy and regional development policy.
Cancelling CEIP without any notice to the industry, without any consultation with the people involved, reminds me of this government's decision to close CFB Summerside. It was about one year ago, April 27 last year, that the government announced the closure of CFB Summerside, which is close to my riding of Malpe-que, P.E.I.
The people of Summerside, in fact all Islanders, are feeling the effects that decision and will be feeling it for some time.
This government must realize that it cannot make major decisions that have sweeping effects on whole regions, such as the decision to close CFB Summerside, without considering alternatives and consulting the people involved.
This government's lack of planning has left an entire region of my province in limbo. People have been waiting for approximately one year for a firm federal commitment of jobs. For the past year, the people of Summer-side and surrounding area have been working hard to save the base and to keep the economic security of their region intact. These people deserve nothing short of total admiration and praise from this House, for they are working against a government which does not plan ahead, which has not fulfilled its year-old commitment for jobs, and which, for all intents and purposes, does not listen to the people of my province.
The government must start to plan ahead with and for the people who will be affected by its decisions.
In the case of the cancellation of CEIP, the Canadian Exploration Incentive Program, as in the case of CFB Summerside, this government offered no alternatives and it failed to consult with the people involved. Furthermore, it failed to honour a well publicized commitment that it would give six months' notice of any change in this program. I will deal with the cancellation of this program more fully in a moment.
First, I want to describe the importance of the mining industry to Canada and the world. In terms of worldwide production, Canada is the third largest producer of minerals in the world. We are the world's foremost exporter. In fact, the mineral industry exports about 80
Government Orders
per cent of its production. In 1988, mineral production was valued at approximately $21 billion.
Before these minerals can be exported, they must be found and then processed, which provides the Canadian economy with about 150,000 direct jobs and many more indirect jobs. Some 120 communities, mainly in the north and remote regions, depend on mining.
The mining industry, mining communities, and the government all realize that mineral exploration is a very risky business. It requires enormous capital investment. Prospectors and developers are at the mercy of our country's geology and the world market. It is that high-level risk in mineral exploration that makes conventional investment very difficult to find. That is why governments over the years have provided various programs and allowances to offset that relatively high risk. CEIP, the program that has just been cancelled, and the Mining Exploration Depletion Allowance were both designated with this in mind.
The energy minister, in a speech to the annual convention of Prospectors and Developers Association in 1988, had this to say regarding the two programs, CEIP and MEDA, and the mining sector: "they make the sector more competitive as an investment vehicle. In terms of investment vehicles there is nothing to match flow-through shares." That is what the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources said in March, 1989.
About one year after he made that statement, the government cancelled the program, which was the only mining exploration incentive program in Canada.
Flow-through shares have been around for a long while, in fact, since 1954. It was not until the introduction of the MEDA program by the Liberal government in 1983 that they were widely used by junior, or smaller, mining companies. This program was started in 1983 and was a very popular program. It was started by the Liberal government of the day, it was popular with the industry and yet this government eliminated it in 1987.
In 1988 the government openly recognized the importance of supporting these junior companies when it introduced the CEIP program. It recognized that the government had to act to maintain a healthy level of exploration in the Canadian mining industry. In May of 1988 CEIP was announced. Its purpose was to help these junior companies raise the equity they require, with the

April 25, 1990
Government Orders
hope that in turn they would do the exploration and the development that Canada needed.
The program actually began in 1989.1 know there were problems in the beginning with the complexity of the program. It took some time before the industry was able to work through all the complicated arrangements. Once they did, they started to use it. In fact, of the $750 million spent in 1989 on mineral exploration, approximately one-half, or $375 million, was generated by flowthrough shares.
Yet this government claims that CEIP was not that popular with junior mining companies. If the program was not fully utilized in 1989, it is largely because the industry was still becoming familiar with the complexity of the program. They were learning how to take the best advantage of it.
There are other reasons why 1989 exploration figures are lower than 1988. First of all, we had the effects of the elimination of MEDA. Then we had the investors who were trying to cope with the aftermath of tax reform. Of course, we had the 1987 stock market crash. The government cancelled this program after one year, citing apathy on the part of the industry as the reason. That is bad policy and it also shows bad faith. The cancellation of CEIP means that junior companies will lack sufficient investor incentives to raise the capital they need to explore.
The government has failed to provide any alternatives to this program, as was the case with the closing of CFB Summerside. It provided no alternatives and did not consult with the people involved. What we have today in the mining industry in 1990 is the same situation we had in 1988 when the government announced this program. At that time the existing 100 per cent write-off was not enough to raise the necessary money for mining exploration because it is a risky business. It was not enough then and it is not enough today.
What we are likely going to see is a decline in Canada's base metal reserves. We are also seeing the end of mineral development agreements such as the one between Ottawa and the province of Ontario. The timing of the cancellation of the program could not have been worse. But it is worse when one considers the fact that the government had promised that any changes in the program would follow after six months' notice and that
the industry would be notified six months ahead of any changes. This did not happen.
The government promised it as recently as December, 1989. In an Energy Department publication called "CEIP Explained", it stated: "A minimum of six months' notice will be given prior to any change (in CEIP)". But less than five months after that promise the government cancelled CEIP without ever notifying the industry that it was being cancelled.
I think it is important that hon. members know what people in the industry are saying about the cancellation of this program. The President of the British Columbia and Yukon Chamber of Mines stated: "The (loss of CEIP) is going to have a dramatic effect on the exploration by small companies". The Prospectors and Developers Association of Canada said: "The cancellation of CEIP will render flow-through shares unmarketable, and the junior mining sector will collapse".
Those are quotes by people in the industry that certainly show the seriousness of cancelling this very important program to the mining industry in Canada. At the very best there will be a real loss of exploration incentive and that will lead to a decline in exploration and development of base metals and other mineral reserves. Such a decline will lead to fewer exports and fewer and lower export revenues.
What we will probably export, however, is not minerals but jobs, because there is a world-wide demand for minerals which will be easily met by other countries who will be eager to meet the demand.
Our reserves are already falling. From 1981 to 1988, even with the incentive provided under MEDA, Canada's reserves of base metals such as copper, zinc, nickel and lead registered declines ranging from 20 per cent to 34 per cent. Between 1988 and 1989 lead reserves did increase about 4 per cent and zinc by 2 per cent. At the same time, copper and nickel reserves fell by 2 per cent and 5 per cent respectively.
An article that appeared this week in the Ottawa Citizen quotes an energy department official as saying: "We're not out of the woods yet in regards to replenishing our reserves". Officials said any progress we are making now is far from enough to maintain our production into the 1990s. In fact, the Department of Energy estimates that simply replenishing Canada's mineral
April 25, 1990

reserves-I am not talking about expanding them, I am simply talking about holding the line-will require an annual expenditure of at least $1.3 billion a year.
In 1989 about half of that amount of about $750 million was spent in exploration. The Prospectors and Developers Association estimates that the total for 1990 will probably fall .to about $610 million. It expects exploration in 1991 to fall even further. It is readily apparent that Canada needs to give some kind of assistance for the mining sector to maintain a healthy level of base metal and other reserves. Certainly, that requires a federal commitment.
Madam Speaker, I know my time is running out. In talking about this whole mining area and the cancellation of CEIP which will mean less money going to remote northern areas, that there is a very human element involved here. Small northern and remote towns in Ontario, Quebec, British Columbia, and elsewhere depend on a healthy mining industry. Certainly that is going to suffer as the result of the loss of CEIP.
I think this government's action contrasts sharply with the tradition of government support of the mining industry in the country, a tradition the Liberal party helped continue and one to which this party remains committed.

Madam Speaker, I want to thank the hon. member for the question. I am always pleased to talk about my province of Prince Edward Island.
Bill C-69 will have very negative effects in P.E.I. I think the area which will cause the greatest damage is the freeze on transfer payments, that is the Established Program Financing, money given to the provinces to look after health services and education.

Prince Edward Island will end up with $13 million less in 1990-91. What does that mean to our education and health system on Prince Edward Island? If the provincial government is getting less money from the federal government, it has either to raise taxes or to cut services. What the federal government has done is transfer part of the debt onto the provincial governments.
The government has to cut services and it has to raise taxes. If it cuts services, the Government of Prince Edward Island will have to cut funding to educational institutions. Tuition fees may have to be higher. Certainly, that is something that the students on Prince Edward Island are very concerned about.
Two weeks ago, I was pleased to take part in a demonstration of Prince Edward Island students where several hundred had gathered to express their concern about government cutbacks in transfer payments, because of a number of things: the transfer payments, the GST, and the cutback to the Challenge Program this year which means that fewer university students are going to have jobs this summer. The students are also upset about the student loan program. They are concerned about the transfer payments, because it may mean that the quality of education will go down. It may mean higher tuition fees. They are concerned about the GST because, for the first time, we are going to have a tax on learning. It will mean 7 per cent on books, supplies and services. If they get their hair cut, they are going to have to pay 7 per cent on that.
It is at a time when students these days are feeling really strapped, because certainly there are real problems with the student loan program. Here again, the government comes in with 7 per cent and puts a tax on learning.
It is also going to affect health care. Are the sick and disabled in the province of Prince Edward Island going to have to suffer? I certainly would hope not, but when the federal government is passing less money to the province, the province will have to increase the tax or cut services. If it cuts services, that is certainly going to affect the people who are sick and disabled.
We have the transfer payments. The hon. member asked me was how the legislation was going to affect the province of Prince Edward Island. I talked about the transfer payments, and their effect on education and

health, and about the students and their concern with the GST.
There is also a lot of concern by small business about the GST. We all know it is a very complex taxation that is coming in. A lot of small businesses are going to have to buy new equipment, such as new cash registers. They are going to have to have new accounting systems. I talked to the owner of a restaurant in my district of Malpeque last week. He was talking to me about the GST. He said: "Look, I run a restaurant. It is a very marginal business. I really cater to the working poor. They come in once or twice a week and buy a hot hamburger or a hot chicken sandwich." He said: "When that 7 per cent comes in, my clients are not going to have any money to buy a hot hamburger because that money is going to be gone on the 7 per cent to pay for the children's clothing, their haircuts, or whatnot." He went to say: "On top of that, for the money that I do take in, I am going to have to keep track of all the tax and submit that tax to the government every so often. I am going to have to get a new accounting system and a new cash register. I might as well pack it up and go work for somebody else".
That attitude has been expressed to me several times in the riding. Small businesses are really feeling the policies of the government, policies which are not helping small business in any way. I would think that the government should be helping small business because it is small business that provides the jobs. people of the area in limbo. They do not know whether an industry will be coming in to provide a job for them or whether they should think of moving off the island and selling their homes. It is the uncertainty. It has created a lot of-
