Madam Speaker, I rise to talk about this bill because I think it is one of the pieces of legislation that is going to have a profound long-term effect on Canada.
Canada is a country that has a few veiy distinct characteristics, one of which has been our approach to basic services for people, services such as education, social services, income support programs, and health care. Particularly when we compare ourselves to the United States, one of the ways in which there is a tremendous distinction is the fact that the federal government has always had a role and responsibility in these areas. Its responsibility and role has been more than just providing funding. Canada has developed a system on a national basis that is known as our safety net.
In terms of people in dire difficulties, those with health problems or illness, loss of income, who need other types of social services or people seeking education, particularly at the post-secondary level, this bill is the starting of the erosion of those fundamental services. I think that we must recognize that this is the logical follow-up of the free trade agreement. This is the beginning of the level playing-field. This is the beginning of the erosion of our social services and health care system and all the things that the government unilaterally denied were under attack in the free trade deal.
The government said our social services were untouchable and now it brings in this type of legislation. It has already dealt a severe blow to our unemployment insurance program. It said: "Of course, our national health care schemes are not under attack." Now, it brings in this type of legislation which clearly is intended to erode these programs on a national basis. One could spend all one's time talking about the impact that these reductions in funds had on any one of these program areas.
April 25, 1990

The provincial premiers have stated that this type of unilateral changing of federal-provincial fiscal programs is tremendously detrimental to provinces and the provinces' abilities to provide services. The province of British Columbia is facing a deficit this year of $650 million. It is not in a position simply to pick up and replace the money being eroded by this legislation.
I would like to spend a few minutes looking at the whole business of the Canada Assistance Plan. I think it is important when we talk about national unity in the country to look at the part the Canada Assistance Plan has played in Canada in developing those kinds of social safety nets that have held the country together allowed people to move within Canada, from one region to another, and still be entitled to benefits.
The Canada Assistance Plan sets out very clearly in its preamble that: "Whereas the Parliament of Canada recognizes the provision of adequate assistance to, in respect of persons in need, and the prevention and removal of the cause of poverty and dependence on public assistance are the concerns of all Canadians". That is what the preamble says. It is the concern of the Canadian Parliament, not the provinces, that the focus is on, not only providing for people in need, but removal of the causes of poverty and dependence on public assistance. It goes on to say that: "It is desirous of encouraging the further development and extension of assistance in welfare service programs throughout Canada."
There are two fundamental parts to the Canada Assistance Act. One deals with income maintenance programs and the other deals with welfare services. There are a number of things that we should look at. With the income assistance program, the Canada Assistance Plan unified the country. Prior to the introduction of the Canada Assistance Plan, we used to have all kinds of things like residential requirements for someone wanting to draw welfare or income assistance. Municipalities were administering income assistance programs. They had to chase around to try to find out where someone was a resident because they would be held responsible for the cost of income assistance.
The Canada Assistance Plan was used as a mechanism of saying to people in Canada: "You have the ability to
Government Orders
move from one area of the country in order to pursue jobs, to pursue a better lifestyle, or to be near family, and you are still entitled to receive income assistance". The costs would be picked up and shared between the provinces and the federal government.
It also did away with the concept of categorical assistance. Assistance must be granted based on need, and not based on some arbitrary determination that you are just and worthy, as under the Elizabethan poor laws. It was based on the fundamental concept that income assistance was to be granted to people who were in need.
Included in the Canada Assistance Plan was the right to appeal. It was a right to appeal which said that a person was not being granted this as a charity but as a right, with the legal recourse of an appeal procedure and, if necessary, access to the courts.
The concept of a national program of income support based on legislation and a right to appeal is diametrically opposed to the charity style of income maintenance programs found in the United States. It is an area in which Canada can be justly proud. This piece of legislation, which is curtailing expenditures in the three largest provinces, is going to affect well over half of all income recipients in Canada.
This is at a time when we have 1.2 million children living in poverty. This is at a time when, in the province of British Columbia, income assistance rates for a mother with two children allow her to feed her children for only two and a half weeks each month. She must depend on other sources of income, on food banks, on neighbours and even on schools for the rest of the month.
In the city of Vancouver and in my own municipality schools are having to feed children. That is not the intent of educational institutions in this country. Because of the cut-backs by this government and provincial governments, particularly governments like the Socred government, schools are having to provide basic necessities.
The Canada Assistance Plan under its assistance provisions also provides other types of services to people who are in need or who are on income assistance. It provides basic medical care, all types of medical care, including access to prescriptions and specialized medical care. It also allows for rehabilitation and getting people

April 25, 1990
Government Orders
who are on income assistance back into the workforce where they can become independent.
It allows for training programs to train people for jobs, for jobs that we often have difficulty filling in this country. Some of the better programs have trained people to work as care aids in hospitals or in long-term care facilities, as well as to work in day care centres.
Sometimes we use our income assistance provisions not only to help people to become independent, but to provide much needed resources in the community.
Other parts of the Canada Assistance Plan refer to basic child welfare services. These are protection services to investigate children who have been abused and neglected, and to provide counselling services for those children or, in extreme cases, alternative living arrangements.
In the last number of years Canadian society has become more and more aware of the inadequacy of our services to children. Basic child welfare services are often tremendously strained. We have just begun to understand the long term effects on people who have been involved in abuse, particularly sexual abuse.
One of the factors that emerges continually when we begin to examine many of the horrendous stories of sexual abuse is that many of the adults who are involved in abuse were themselves abused as children. We can all sit back and say how deplorable their behaviour is, and we can condemn them. But in many of the cases we should be condemning ourselves. These are the children who, if they had been provided the proper counselling services 15 years ago, if our child welfare services had been adequate, would not be the adults now engaged in abusive conduct.
I have worked in social services and corrections all my life. I have been involved in juvenile courts, juvenile street programs and juvenile prostitution. I have also been involved with teachers. There are very few Grade 1, 2 and 3 teachers who cannot tell you who are the children in trouble, which families are having difficulty, or who needs the services that are provided under the Canada Assistance Plan. They will tell you that if these services are not provided now, society is going to pay more in the future. This, in my 25 years, is something I have watched, regrettably.
I have known children who have grown up to be notorious criminals who are serving 25 or 30 years in jail. I worked with them at a time when it was said: "Let's provide more resources to this family now. It will cost us maybe $4,000 or $5,000 to provide proper counselling services, or day care so that the mother has a break, or drug counselling that is necessary to make sure that a person does not become a chronic addict". Yet the money was not provided.
Now we pay $50,000 a year to keep that person in a federal penitentiary. We will pay an equal amount to keep that person in a mental hospital. We will pay money to keep that person's family on income assistance.
The services that are provided under the Canada Assistance Plan are basic services. We are not talking about frills. Under the Canada Assistance Plan it defines what are welfare services. It states that welfare services mean: "-services having as their object the lessening, removal or prevention of the cause and effects of poverty, child neglect or dependence on public assistance". Then it lists some of the services.
The general thrust of the Canada Assistance Plan is to deal with child neglect and poverty. I cannot understand why a government would attack such fundamental programs. Its members stand up and say: "We want to deal with drug addiction. We want to deal with family violence. We want to deal with child poverty, child abuse and child neglect". That is what they say, but then they bring in legislation that is the first step to the total destruction of Canada's system of economic underpinning to provide such services on a national basis.
Other services that are provided are rehabilitation services, adoption services, homemaker services, day care, community development services, consulting and research. These are the fundamental services that form the structure of Canada's safety net.
I come back to the point that this legislation is not just legislation dealing with a restriction of transfer payments to the provinces. It is the beginning of an attack on our fundamental services. Obviously, it flows out of the free trade deal by which we must harmonize our social programs with those of the United States.
April 25, 1990

In the time I have left I want to talk a bit about one of the other sections covered in this legislation. I refer to the Established Programs Financing. This bill is attacking two of the other fundamental structures of Canadian society, that is health care and post-secondary education.
The province of British Columbia is in a crisis in health care. We do not have adequate health care facilities. We have a shortage of health staff.
In my municipality it is more than just a crisis, it is an absolute disaster. Surrey now has 1.67 acute care beds per 100,000 people. If you take out people who should be in long-term care facilities, that figure is reduced to 1.3. The target for the province is 3.3 beds per 100,000. The average in British Columbia is 3.8 beds per 100,000. In the City of Vancouver it is 6.4. We have less than one-third of the hospital beds that we need.
What is the impact on my community and my constituents? In closing, I will point out what the impact is. Nearly 50 per cent of the people in that municipality have to travel elsewhere for basic health care services. There are now nearly 3,000 people on the waiting list for beds in the hospital.
This government chooses to attack this type of program, simply making it impossible for fast-growing municipalities like Surrey to ever catch up in providing basic health care to the residents who so desperately need it.

speakeroldname: Mr. Pierre H. Vincent (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, it is with great pleasure that I rise to speak to Bill C-69, which follows from the budget tabled in February. That budget, hon. members will remember, had many great advantages, among which was the fact that for the first time in many years, no increases whatsoever in taxes were announced. I think it is important to mention it, because we too often hear about the budgets the federal government has tabled since 1984 and all the tax increases they contained. Unfortunately, we do not insist enough on the fact that this governement was able to introduce a budget with no tax increase for the first time in many, many years, after tabling in 1988 a budget providing for a reduction in income tax for low-income individuals and an increase in corporate tax. Also, as you will remember, we introduced a minimum tax for high-income Cana-
Government Orders
dians who were legally using tax shelters. This year, even if they still benefit from tax shelters, they do have to pay their fair share of tax.
That budget must be looked at as a whole, and Bill C-69 is part of it. Our fiscal policy dates from 1984. You will recall that, in 1984, when the Conservative government was elected, there was a $200 billion debt left by our friends opposite. The $200 billion national debt was financed by borrowings and interest payments were huge.
But even more serious, Madam Speaker, in 1984, the federal government, the Government of Canada, was spending each year $16 billion more than what it was getting in tax revenue. The government of the day was therefore running an annual deficit of $16 billions in program spending.
This year, this Conservative government now in office will spend $9 billion less than it brings in, the amounts payable in interests excluded once again. That is a $25 billion turnaround over a period of five years, Madam Speaker.
That is why we can say, Madam Speaker, as the Minister of Finance did rightly, that in four years from now, our annual deficit which adds to our national debt every year, will be reduced by half. That is important, because it shows that we are finally on the right course to bring down our annual deficit to zero, for one thing. The moment that is achieved, we will finally start-I hear my colleague laugh, Madam Speaker, but it is a fact-paying not our debts but those left us in 1984 by that government who was spending, I repeat, $16 billion more money yearly that it brought in.
You can understand, as do all of those Canadians who are listening, that if they spend $16,000 more then what they earn, they will eventually end up in an intolerable situation.
Madam Speaker, that is the total picture. Since 1984, it is true that there has been cuts. Since 1984, there has been tax hikes. But, what we must keep in mind, Madam Speaker, is that those cuts made since 1984 account for 70 per cent of the redution of the annual deficit, which was at $39 billion in 1984.
Only 30 per cent of the decifit reduction comes from tax hikes. It is important to mention it. The expenditure control plan tabled in 1990 accounts for 60 per cent of all 1990-1991 government expenditures, which made it

April 25, 1990
Government Orders
possible to save $3 billion the first year and $4 billion the next.
Yet, it should be emphasized that exemptions are provided for under the expenditure control plan. For instance, Old Age Security pensions will not be affected and will continue to increase; the same with the Guaranteed Income Supplement and the family allowances.
The expenditure control plan will not affect the amount received by low income Canadian men and women.
But all the rest will be affected, which means that 60 per cent of total federal expenditures will be reduced under the budget plan tabled in 1990. As you know, Madam Speaker, Bill C-69, which flows from that budget plan, affects transfer payments to provinces. We know there are two important programs that give money to all provinces. There is the established programs financing, which applies to all provinces. Under this program, each province receives a certain sum on a per capita basis. It is a fair and equitable program for all provinces.
The other program that we know, particularly in the province of Quebec, is equalization. Under this program, the federal government gives money to provinces that are considered poorer, in addition to the money they receive under the other program. Those provinces are the Maritimes, Quebec, Manitoba and, some years, Saskatchewan. If you look at the situation since 1984 and up to 1990, the amount paid to the provinces by the federal government has increased, on average, by 6.5 per cent a year. At the same time, other expenditures of the Canadian government have increased only by 3.6 per cent a year. We see, therefore, that the federal government, which has a huge accumulated debt and a deficit just starting to be under control, has transferred annually more money to the provinces that it has spent. Transfers to the provinces, Madam Speaker, will amount this year to $35 billion. A quarter of all the money spent by the Canadian government goes directly to the provinces: $35 billion this year.
We must look at the Canadian reality. Referring to the Canadian government deficit, may be very nice, but if you are a foreign investor, Madam Speaker, and you look at what you would like to do in Canada, you will consider
the Canadian government deficit, and you also will consider the situation in each and every province. And you will find that interests on the debt in provinces eat up an average of 12 cents on each dollar of revenue, that is the amount of interest paid by provinces-12 cents on the dollar. But turning to the Canadian government, the rate is 35 cents on the dollar. Which means the Canadian government, out of each and every revenue dollar, must pay 35 cents in interest not to repay the principal but simply to cover the interests.
That is because of your incompetence.

Madam Speaker, looking at transfers to provinces in 1984-85, under the Established Programs Financing among others.
In 1984-85, the provinces received $14,5 billion from the federal government. In 1989-90, they will receive $20 billion. So, they will receive a lot more money they can spend the way they want. They don't have to account for it to the federal government. On the other hand this government, this Parliament, must report to the Canadian people every time it raises taxes. I think that that major increase of funds is in line with the needs of the provinces but it is also necessary to limit its increase in
April 25, 1990

the face of the astronomical federal debt threatening the future of our nation.
Again and again, opposition members ask for more money, less taxes, and God knows what. But we must face facts and be realistic. Appropriate measures must be taken now so that we do not end up in an absolutely unbearable situation two, three or five years down the road. It is not normal for a country such as ours to be as heavily in debt as it is, considering its population. Steps have been taken since 1984 to ensure that we get back on track. The effort that we are requiring from the population with the cuts and the tax hikes is a collective effort on the part of all Canadians. We are asking everyone of them, whatever the province they live in, to share in this collective effort, as well as the provincial governments, which have also spent much more than the federal government since 1984. If we look at the rate of increase of their spendings, we see that it is almost double that of the federal government spendings.
There is a certain lack of logic in having the federal government collect taxes from Canadians, take the money, give it without any conditions to the provinces and tighten its belt while the provinces increase their expenditures. I can understand why they spend more because the needs are increasing. But Canada as a country has a debt and we must all work on it together, as individuals, provincial governments, social groups and everyone else, to make Canada less indebted in future and in the hope that one day the debt will be gone and we can do something with the money now being wasted.
Just think that it costs us $35 billion a year in interest. How many programs and organizations could be helped with the $35 billion now being wasted on interest? Again, on a debt left to us by the former government which spent-
You doubled the debt!

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
-thoughtlessly for 20 years. We are trying to pick up the pieces. We are trying desperately, with everyone's help, to solve this debt problem, because we are accused of doubling the national debt. It is a simple calculation. When we were elected, the debt was $200 billion. Ten per cent of that is $20 billion. Two hundred billion at 10 per cent gives $20 billion in interest we had to pay, not on our debts but on the debts you left.

However, those $20 billion increased the deficit instead of being used to help Canadians. And my colleagues criticized the GST!
Madam Speaker, the present federal sales tax is more than 65 years old. When I was doing my masters degree in tax law more than 10 years ago, our professor said: "This tax is bad for the country! We keep hoping every year the Liberal government will change it". Madam Speaker, the Liberal government at the time never had the political courage to bring about this change.
The GST is a good thing for Canada and for Quebec. At last our industries will be able to get ahead, go outside the country and compete with foreign industries that come and try to sell their goods here. And it will be fair and equitable. It will be fair and equitable for Canadians, including Canadians on low incomes.
Those with an income of $30,000 or less will benefit under the GST, Madam Speaker. They will have more money in their pockets at the end of the year then they had this year.
Mr. Speaker, I would urge my colleagues on the other side of the House to read a number of articles on the subject that appeared in La Presse, where the figures were given by an experienced journalist, without political overtones. He proved, providing the appropriate figures and examples, that to people with an income of $30,000 or less the meant was a net gain at the end of the year. Those are not my words, Madam Speaker. That is what was said in an article that appeared in La Presse a few weeks ago. I urge my colleagues to read that article. It is very instructive.
Madam Speaker, in concluding, Bill C-69 must be passed as soon as possible. I hope my colleagues across the way will vote in favour of the bill so that we can proceed with the financial and administrative reorganization of the Canada they left us in 1984.

Madam Speaker, Bill C-69, which is before the House today, is a devastating indictment of this government. It is a sorry state of affairs that this government, in the name of debt reduction, should devastate two particular areas that

April 25, 1990
Government Orders
have always been considered very sacred in this country. I refer to the areas of health and education.
Bill C-69 is typical of the pass the buck philosophy of the present government. Instead of taking on its responsibilities, it has passed them on to the provinces. This is the third time since this government came into office in 1984 that it has attacked the Establish Programs Financing. Either the provinces will have to raise their taxes or the hospitals and education systems will have to absorb the costs.
The total loss to the provinces over the next five years will be $7.4 billion. If we add the two previous cuts announced by the government, we find that the cumulative reduction in federal contributions from 1986-87 to 1994-95 amounts to $31.1 billion.
On March 24, 1982, the current Minister of Finance said in this House: "Let us not make hospitals, universities and colleges a battleground between the federal government and the provincial governments. Let us solve those problems outside of the arena."
Yet that same member, who is now the Minister of Finance, has brought forward a budget that does exactly those things.
With respect to post-secondary education, the Prime Minister betrayed once again his own promise to have first-class education for our youth. In so doing, he made a mockery of the national task force on education that he himself created.
I quote a statement from the Prime Minister: "This government will carry its fair share of the burden to ensure that all young Canadians receive a first-class education as they confront a world-class challenge." That statement was made by the Prime Minister on August 25, 1989.
Also under Bill C-69, growth under the Canada Assistance Program will be limited. Under CAP the federal and provincial governments share equally in the costs of welfare payments and basic necessities such as food, shelter, clothing, dental care for the poor and essential services for the disabled. This is the first time in the 24-year history of the program that CAP has been limited. Ontario, Alberta and B.C. are the only three provinces to have a limit. Does the government think for one minute that the poor in Ontario are less poor than the poor in Quebec? To me, poor is poor is poor, regardless of which province you come from in this country.
The Canadian Exploration Incentive Program, which provides for a grant of 30 per cent of the cost of resource exploration-mining, oil and gas-financed with flowthrough shares, was cancelled as of budget day. The elimination of CEIP will have a devastating impact on primary exploration in Canada, with junior exploration firms bearing the brunt. We can expect a substantial reduction in mineral exploration at a time when Canada needs to replenish its dwindling base metal reserves. Already in 1989 the amount spent on exploration was down from $1.2 billion in 1988.
This is another broken promise by this government. On May 3, 1988, the Minister of State for Forestry and Mines said: "This rate, 30 per cent, will be guaranteed for two years until the end of 1990, after which the rate maybe adjusted." Can we ever believe anything that the government tells us?
Under Bill C-69 public utilities income tax transfers are frozen. The Public Utilities Income Tax Transfer Act provides for the transfer to provinces of 95 per cent of the federal income tax collected from certain privately owned electric and gas utilities. Transfers will be frozen for two years at the 1989-90 levels, reducing projected expenditures under the act by $16 million in 1990-91 and $34 million in 1991-92. PUITT was implemented in 1986 and its purpose was to put private electric and gas companies, which pay federal tax, on an equal footing with Crown corporations in the resource sector, which do not pay tax.
Canadians have every right to be cynical about this government. We in the Liberal party oppose Bill C-69. Interest rates are high, and if this government continues with its present policies more unemployment will be created. Provinces will be less able to cope. The people who are less able to cope, who are the poor, the handicapped and the sick, will suffer the most. The government is asking those people to help reduce the deficit, one which it has doubled since coming into office, while others are getting off scot-free.
This government has lost all sense of propriety and this is a reflection of the extreme limits to which it will go to force its will on the people.

Madam Speaker, I am very happy to enter the debate this afternoon on Bill C-69.
April 25, 1990

Bill C-69 looks rather innocuous. It is just a few pages with a nice title on it. It has all the proper logos and the Minister of Finance has his name at the bottom. It really looks very straightforward, very simple.
I suppose in one respect it is very simple. The bill is entitled, "An act to amend certain statutes to enable restraint of government expenditures". That is another way of saying that this is a bill to dismantle Canada. This is a bill to begin the destruction of what we know as being Canadian. I do not think the title is very accurate. The government missed the boat there. Maybe it should have said that this is the beginning of the end of Canada as we know it act, or this is a bill that begins to undo what Canadians have struggled to achieve for, in some cases, generations. There is a whole set of more appropriate titles than the one given to Bill C-69.
I have listened with interest to the previous speakers, and I can only assume that Conservative members have not visited their constituencies in the last few months because if they had they would know what the people of Canada are saying.
For example, one item in the bill refers to the Canadian Exploration Incentives Program Act. This is a program which for many years provided incentives and encouragement for those people who go prospecting for new mineral deposits. That is what much of the basis of our economy is built on, particularly in British Columbia. Mining is our number two industry. It is second in importance in terms of employment, investment and attracting capital into our part of Canada. But, of course, it depends upon those people who go out and explore.
Exploration companies normally are small companies. They tend to be Canadian-owned companies. They tend to keep their money in Canada, in their communities, and provide employment for people to seek out new mineral deposits and then develop them into potential ore bodies for production. In other words, they are the lifeblood of the mining industry.
The government has decided to take away encouragement, support and incentive for these folks. These are people of whom we as Canadians are proud, because they take those Beaver airplanes up into the north and hike and live in the muskeg and so on. They discover
Government Orders
what has made this country known around the world for its huge mineral deposits and developments.
But the government no longer wants to encourage people to do that. As you know, Madam Speaker, the statistics indicate that mining exploration in Canada has fallen off in the natural gas and oil sectors, as well as in the mining sector. So exploration activity in all of the primary resource areas is falling off because of the high interest rates. The stock markets are also falling so we cannot look to the stock market for a place to raise revenue for exploration.
While the whole bottom is falling out of the exploration business, the government says: "We have a great idea. We are going to cause even more pain. We are going to inflict more suffering on to this critical sector of the economy by pulling out our support". One wonders what on earth would motivate a government at this critical time in the mining industry to make life worse for those people who seek out new mineral deposits.
That is not the worst of it. I find it passing strange when I look through this bill to find that the government has come up with what it thinks is an appropriate idea for the 1990s, and that is to cut back support for young people going into education.
When looking around the world and, in particular, at all European countries, one sees that nations are investing in their young people. They are investing in their universities, colleges, vocational schools, technical schools, and training institutes. They realize that to invest in their young people-and to reinvest in those who are not young people anymore but require new skills to meet the demands of a knowledged-based economy of the 1990s-they have to invest in their colleges, universities, and post-secondary institutions.
Europe is doing that. Countries in the Far East, such as Japan which is a major competitor on the international markets, are investing heavily in what they know is their most important resource, their people. We have to be the only country in the world that is going to reduce support for education, that is going to reduce the funding that we normally would give to our universities and colleges. I find that almost unbelievable.
I must tell you a little story, Mr. Speaker. Over the last few weeks I made a point of visiting a number of high schools in my constituency. I visited Kamloops Secondary School, North Kamloops Secondary School, Chase

April 25, 1990
Government Orders
Secondary School, Logan Lake Secondary School, Bar-riere Secondary School and Clearwater Secondary School as well as Caribou University College.
I had a chance to meet with students informally and to address some larger assemblies as well. I asked whether they would believe that there is a government in the world that is curtailing its support for education. They said they could not believe that and wondered what backward country that would be. I asked whether they could believe that there is a government now in the western industrialized nations that is cutting back on support for student loans and that is now imposing user fees for those students who want to obtain a loan.
This was the one that really caught their attention, Mr. Speaker. You will love this one. I asked if they knew what country in the world is now imposing a tax on reading. There is only one in the whole world. The students did not know which it was. I said that it is Canada. The Government of Canada is imposing a tax on literature; on newspapers, magazines and books. This is the only country in the entire world doing this.
I think we are also the only country in the world that has now imposed a user fee for those young people who need to borrow to pursue education. We know education is very expensive these days. It is a $ 10,000-a-year ticket for a single person to go off to college or university. Not many people can afford $10,000 a year to go to university, college, or vocational school. If one have two or three children in one's home, that is a lot of money. We depend on the ability of young people to go out to work in the summers so that they can derive income to at least pay part of their way along with loans, bursaries and, perhaps, help from friends and family.
What government do you think, Mr. Speaker, curtailed investment in summer work programs for young people? What government do you think decided to cut back on the Challenge 90 program, a program to encourage the private sector, the non-profit sector, and the public sector to hire students in the summer so that they can afford to go on for post-secondary education? Do you know what government cut back on that by 30 per cent in my constituency this year? It was the federal government.
It is bordering on madness when the Government of Canada says it is going to cut back on support for students' summer programs, it is going to impose a user fee on loans for students, it is going to cut back on funding to the universities, colleges, and vocational schools across the country, and it is going to tax reading.
No wonder students are standing around a little dazed these days wondering what on earth is coming next. I suspect they get up in the morning and dread reading the newspaper to find out what the federal government is going to be doing next to the young people of the country.
Do the Conservative members in the House of Commons realize what is in Bill C-69? Do they support this notion of cutting back support to the colleges and universities across the country at a time when every other country with which we compete is investing heavily in these areas? I do not think they do. I encourage my friends opposite to at least look at this bill before we are asked to vote on it later today.
What would you think, Mr. Speaker, of a government that says: "We have to pick on somebody now and we have decided to pick on sick people"? What kind of a government would it be in a country that picks on sick people? What would one think of a government that says to the poorer provinces: "Rather than assist you, as a central government should, in the development of your health care system in terms of your hospitals and your long-term care facilities, which would give relatively equal access to decent health care across the country, we are going to begin to curtail our support"?
If one is sick in some parts of the country, particularly in a have-not province, one will not have the same access to decent health care as one would in a wealthy province. Do we want a Canada where health care is available at a reasonably high level in certain parts of Canada and at a lesser level in other parts of Canada?
The reason the federal government got involved in the first place was to provide uniform health care across the country. It did not matter whether one was sick in Nova Scotia, Manitoba or Ontario. One would get the same medical treatment. One would have the same access to quality health care. But this government said: "We are
April 25, 1990

now going to abandon that tradition". What kind of an uncaring government would do that?
A Tory government.

As my friend says, a Conservative government. I can only assume that that is the government that is doing it. It is cutting back on health care and cutting back on support for sick people in the country.
This is the same group that took a slap at veterans in hospitals in its budget. It said: "Look, folks, you have to pay more." These are people who were prepared to die for their country, die for what we have struggled to achieve in this country. They were prepared to die. As a result, they are very sick and are now in hospital. Yet, the government says: "We are going to have to charge you folks more." Such actions really make one wonder.
On top of all this, in just a couple of days, these petitions have come in from one constituency, the constituency of Kamloops. These petitions represent people speaking out against the goods and services tax. There are hundreds and hundreds-maybe thousands- of names that have arrived in just a few days.
I see my hon. friend from the Liberal party is here. He knows that the goods and services tax is now before the Liberal Senate.
Thank goodness for a Liberal Senate.

We are counting on it. We realize that the father of the goods and services tax was our good Prime Minister. Now, we have Allan MacEachen as the godfather when it is before the Senate. We will have to see what the Liberal Senate is going to do with the goods and services tax. Time will tell. We will all be watching and waiting with bated breath to see whether or not the Senate does the correct thing.
What else have we got in this legislation? In Bill C-69, the government cuts out support for the mining exploration sector. Then, it decided to cut back on funding for post-secondary education. Of course, what that means is that we perpetuate the hewers of wood and drawers of water type of life-style we have been fighting and struggling to overcome for many years.
Then, the government cuts back on health care funding in this bill. What else could it possibly do? The one area that springs to mind is social services. I refer to programs to help single parents and the poor of Canada.

Surely, the government would not cut back on those programs.
When you get to page 5 of the bill, there it is. The government indicates that it is going to cut back on the Canada Assistance Plan, which means cutting back on social services and social programs for the poorest people in Canada.
One of the banks we have in the country that is thriving in terms of business is the food banks. When you drive through large cities like Toronto you see a lot of McDonald's hamburger places with those golden arches. They seem to be on almost every comer as you drive through the city. Do you know that there are more food banks in Toronto than McDonald's hamburger joints? That is only one city. We have thousands and thousands of people who every day line up to get a food hamper because their social services simply cannot meet the needs of their families.
As members of Parliament, we are all aware that in our own constituencies there are families on social assistance with two or three children and, in particular, single parents, who come to us with escalating rents and escalating costs to say: "By the end of the month, I do not have any money. I have to go to the food bank. I have to go to the thrift shop to get a pair of used running shoes for one of my children".
We have hundreds of thousands of people living on the very edge and, quite frankly, if we are going to be honest, over the edge. On what they receive in social assistance, particularly in the large urban areas, it is simply impossible to sustain those individuals and families.
What is the federal government going to do about that? Is it going to improve that situation? No, it is going to make it worse, it is going to cut back on its support for social services in the country.
I know that some of my friends across the way on the Conservative benches are saying: "That is all right, Mr. Riis, you can go on and talk about this all day, but where is the money going to come from? Where is the money going to come from if we are going to continue education?" Let me make a modest proposal.
Under the tax systems of most countries around the world, when an individual or family receives a huge inheritance of many millions of dollars-perhaps in some cases $10 million or $20 million-they pay tax on that. Canada is one of the few countries in the world where one does not pay any tax if one inherits a large sum of money. I am not talking about somebody inheriting a family farm, a family business or a family house. I

April 25, 1990
Government Orders
am talking about people who end up with a windfall inheritance of many millions of dollars. Not a single penny of income tax has to be paid on that. We say that is not right. If it can be done in other countries like the United States, why do we not do it here in Canada?
Let us look to the United States. In the United States, in 1986, President Reagan noticed that there were thousands and thousands of profitable corporations that did not pay any income tax at all, year after year, and he said that was wrong. He wanted to close that loophole so the President of the United States introduced a minimum corporate tax. Those thousands and thousands of corporations that were making good profits and could use all the fancy loopholes the system, and had first rate tax lawyers and tax accountants to enable them to get into a non-taxable situation, had to pay at least a minimum corporate tax, which generated billions of dollars.
Do you know, Mr. Speaker, that there was not a single corporate spokesperson in the United States who spoke out against that initiative? Not one. I mean, how could one not? If one makes $400 million and is asked to pay a few dollars income tax, how could one say one ought not to be doing that? Not a single person spoke out in any serious way against that initiative.
Why do we not have that in Canada? Why would we not have the same thing in Canada so that those 65,000 profitable corporations that do not pay any income tax whatsoever, year after year, pay their fair share? We are not asking for them to pay exorbitant amounts. We are not asking them to pay significant amounts, just their fair share. If they paid just their fair share, we would generate hundreds of millions of dollars that we do not presently generate to support programs such as helping our young people get a decent education or helping people who are sick have access to long-term care beds.
In the city of Kamloops, we have a major hospital yet I personally know a number of individuals who are waiting months for surgery. There is a list of over 2,000 people waiting for surgery. If one has a heart problem, the province of British Columbia says that one should go down to the United States and have one's operation because we do not have any room. That is not the kind of health care system that we developed in this country.
Our health care system needs to be supported and this bill does exactly the opposite.
I draw to your attention something I came across today. These are some interesting figures, hot off the press, that point out how the tax system in Canada has shifted. Back in 1950, the amount of revenue that came in from corporations and individuals was even, it was balanced. Fifty per cent came from the corporations and 50 per cent from individuals.
Over the years, as a result of a number of Liberal, as well as Conservative governments, this is no longer 50 per cent. It has shifted so that today 79 per cent of the taxes come from individual Canadians and 21 per cent comes from corporations. That is quite a shift over just a handful of years. While individuals have been gouged, gouged, gouged, corporations have been getting a better deal than ever, particularly since the 1950s. Over the years, the corporate sector has been the major beneficiary of our tax system at the expense of individuals, which we are all well aware of.
May I make another suggestion in terms of where we can obtain funds for reducing both our deficit and our debt.
By the way, I noticed with interest the previous speaker in the Conservative benches was concerned about the debt. I have to remind that individual that since the Conservatives have become government in our country, the debt of the country has risen from about $150 billion to nearly $400 billion. In other words, we have seen more than a 100 per cent increase in the country's debt during this particular government.
To talk about their concern, it would not appear they have much concern. If they did, may I suggest something that the government could have done in terms of gaining more revenue?
I have all these petitions against the goods and services tax. One of the reasons that people are concerned about the goods and services tax is because they know the system is unfair. When the system is unfair, an underground economy builds. Some economists now suggest that it is as high as $100 billion in untaxed transactions each year. If the underground economy is that size and was simply taxed at the regular tax rate, that would be the amount of our deficit on an annual basis. That is

what is going to happen, an increasing underground economy.
In closing, I would like to say that obviously we in the New Democratic Party do not support Bill C-69. We do not think that curtailing support for education, health care and social services in this country, particularly during these very difficult times, is the right thing to do. As a matter of fact, it goes against what we know as being Canadian.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to thank you for allowing me to participate in this debate which deals with the government's expenditure restraint act, Bill C-69.
As you will no doubt agree, Mr. Speaker, the Conservative government's record clearly demonstrates a litany of broken promises, of misguided and mean-spirited policies which have attacked average taxpaying Canadians, and left them a little more dispirited and a little more disenfranchised than they were before the Tories came to power.
Canadians have had enough. Indeed, the latest opinion polls confirm that the Prime Minister and his government are the most unpopular government in all of Canadian history. Only 15 per cent of all Canadians support the present administration. With that kind of support, the government ought to be asking itself very serious questions.
Moreover, it should realize that something is seriously wrong. What kind of government would pursue a misguided policy, such as the Government Expenditures Restraint Act, when it knows that it is the most unpopular government in our history? I will tell you what kind of government, Mr. Speaker. One that has lost touch with reality, one that has let power go to its head and one that has a complete disdain for the average Canadian.
The oligarchs of ancient Greece used to say that we are the enemies of the people, and we shall devise all the methods which we can to harm them. Unfortunately, the Conservative government is not nearly so frank. From free trade to the unemployment insurance reform, to the clawback of old age pensions, family allowances, to the goods and services tax, to the cut-backs in VIA Rail, to the cut-backs in veterans' affairs, cut-backs to summer
Government Orders
employment for student programs, the long list of the government's mean-spirited initiatives clearly demonstrates that the government is taking its frustrations out on the backs of the Canadian people.
That is right. The government is frustrated because it has failed to fulfil its promise to balance the budget. The deficit is still hovering around $30 billion yearly, and the government has doubled the national debt since it came to power in 1984. Think of it. This government which preached that it intended to balance the budget and exercise fiscal restraint, has done more to increase the public debt than all other Canadian governments combined. That debt now stands at a walloping $320 billion. After having taken individual Canadians for all they were worth, this government has realized that it would have to find another victim upon which to lay the responsibility for its financial mess. Since it knew that it would never get away with another program cut, or another tax hike, and it realized that its options were limited, it opted to lay the burden of its death on the shoulders of the provinces. The freezing of federal transfers will cost the provinces an estimated $7.4 billion over the next five years. That is a lot of national reconciliation.
As you know, Mr. Speaker, the federal government transfers approximately $24 billion of its $943 billion budget to the provinces under three specific programs. That amount compares with $39.4 billion to service the debt and $32.6 billion in transfers to individuals. Moreover, two of the programs which federal-provincial transfers served to finance are being attacked by Bill C-69, the bill that we are debating today.
First is the Established Program Financing which provides provinces with equal per capita block grants pertaining to the provision of health care and post-secondary education, and second, the Canada Assistance Plan which matches provincial payments for social assistance and social services.
For instance, the cuts to the Established Program Financing will cost the province of New Brunswick $206 million from 1990 to 1995. Looking at the figures from 1986 to 1995 provides an even gloomier scenario. Over that period Conservative policies will have cost the province $1,057 billion. That is not a government which

April 25, 1990
Government Orders
cares for the health and welfare of the people of New Brunswick and of Canadians.
The passage of this legislation will represent the third time that the Conservative government has attacked the Established Programs Financing since 1986. Cumulatively, EPF cut-backs between 1986 and 1995 amount to the astounding sum of $31.1 billion, of which $22.2 billion should have been allocated to health care and $8.9 to post-secondary education.
It is hard to imagine that the government would savagely attack education in Canada in this manner. The Prime Minister claimed at a Progressive Conservative general meeting last August, and I quote:
This government will carry its fair share of the burden to ensure
that all young Canadians will receive a first-class education as they
confront a world-class challenge.
The tragedy is that the Prime Minister's words are contradicted by the actions of this bill. At a time when student enrolment is up by 35 per cent and when operating budgets are down by 19 per cent, the Prime Minister's actions spell disaster for post-secondary education in Canada.
Bill C-69 helps to demonstrate the government's inability to deal with the problems faced by students and young people across Canada. As a result of this legislation, post-secondary education will be faced with harsh alternatives which may include a combination of tax increases and higher education costs in general.
I believe that the Canadian Association of University Teachers summed it up best when its representatives declared that the last budget "makes a mockery of the federal commitment to the young men and women of this country. The magnitude of the reduction is insupportable".
It is obvious that the provinces could make up for any federal cuts to the cost-sharing program out of their general revenues. However, when federal transfers to the provinces are reduced, university budgets generally follow suit. Ultimately it is the students who suffer.
Last February the Association of Universities and Colleges of Canada warned the finance minister in a pre-budget submission to him that cutting transfer payments under the Established Programs Financing would be harmful to provincial grants to overcrowded and under-funded universities.
The Association of Universities and Colleges of Canada's submission observed that federal government support for higher education has declined by 20 per cent since 1977, while university enrolment has increased by 35 per cent over the same period. If this trend continues, there is a definite possibility that the current federal policy of matching grants to universities from private sources will be discontinued when the policy runs out in 1991.
Clearly the government's policies are creating a system whereby only those students who are from the wealthiest backgrounds will be able to aspire to a higher education. It is heart rending to imagine that the Canada our forefathers created, a caring, peaceful, just and tolerant country, will have become an elitist society where only the few can hope to gain from the benefits of a higher education. This trend clearly flies in the face of Canadian tradition, and the government will have to answer for its actions.
Let me remind the government that Canada is a country which values equality of opportunity and social justice. Any government that tampers with these truths runs a considerable risk, indeed.
If this government thinks that it had a hard time with Canadian seniors when it tried to deindex their pensions, just wait until the students begin to protest these cut-backs and the treatment to which they will be subjected if this bill passes.
Time and again we have heard from the Conservative government that Canada must be able to compete in a global economy. Time and again we have heard it said that Canada needed more funding for research and development. Time after time we have heard this government proclaim how much it intended to do to put Canada back on the right track after years of alleged Liberal mismanagement, yet the facts clearly demonstrate their governing philosophy is "Let the fittest survive and the rest will have to make do with less".
The problem with this government is that it likes power too much. It knows it intends to slash social programs, but it cannot bring itself to be frank with the Canadian electorate and tell them because it knows it will tossed out on its ear. But after six years of being told one thing and then being subjected to treatment that is completely at odds with those words, Canadians have had enough. Indeed, the polls indicate that this government is the most unpopular government in history.
April 25, 1990

Canadians are telling this government that they are not impressed. This brings to mind a saying "If you fool me once, shame on you. If you fool me twice, shame on me".
Canadians are onto this government's intentions. They see clearly and they are not being fooled by the Prime Minister's sweet-sounding rhetoric. They know that this government is the one which swore it would never do anything to undermine Canada's unemployment insurance system, and then proceeded to gut it through legislation now before the other place. They know this is the government that promised never to slash VIA Rail services but did so at the first opportunity. They realize that this is a government which promised never to touch old age pensions and family allowances, but clawed them back without so much as a second thought. They realize that this is the most unpopular government in history and are telling themselves that they have had enough and will not put up with it much longer. Canadians are sick and tired of this government.

Finally, Mr. Speaker, total cuts in health care in this bill will amount to $5,247 billion for the next five years. And that is not all, far from it. If we take into account cuts in Established Programs Financing from 1986 to 1995, the total comes to $22,154 billion. You will agree, Mr. Speaker, that these budget cuts are absolutely outrageous.
It is most ironic that the Prime Minister, who as we know admires the American way of doing things, is cutting back on health care financing at a time when Americans are looking with envy at our health care system.
Mr. Speaker, the truth is the Canadian medicare system does not take up more than 8.5 per cent of the National Gross Product, compared to 11.5 per cent in the United States, despite the fact our system is universally socialized. Our system is not perfect but it provides Canadians with the best, the most economical and efficient health care in the world. It is more than popular; 85 per cent of Canadians believe it to be our most important social service. About 60 per cent of the people who responded to a recent survey in the United States said they were in favour of establishing such a system in their country. The Canadian government is nonetheless bent on transforming a program this is the
Government Orders
envy of the whole world into a nightmarish and under-financed program.
Madam Speaker, it is obvious that our medicare system is being axed by this government, and that it will look more and more like the American system. Furthermore, this government is showing us that it wants the provinces, and consequently the middle class and the poor, to pay more taxes. Of all policies put forward by this government, the cuts in medicare are the most reprehensible and repugnant simply because they make health care a luxury. If the provinces decide not to raise their taxes, they will have to pass on the cuts to hospitals, which in turn will be forced to cut the nomber of beds, reduce costly operations, and so on. As a result, Madam Speaker, the Canadian taxpayers will have once again to pay the bill.
It is ironic that this Bill should be introduced by the Minister of Finance who said a few years ago: "Let's not make hospitals, universities and colleges a battleground with the provinces. Let's find a solution outside these fields."
You know, Madam Speaker, power is a strange thing. A famous English writer, Lord Acton, said in this regard: "Power has a tendency to corrupt, and absolute power corrupts absolutely."
However, power does not always exact such a toll. Twenty-four years ago, the Liberal government of Prime Minister Lester Pearson created the Canada Assistance Plan. This agreement provided for a shared financing, between the federal and provincial governments, of social assistance programs.
Nevertheless, the government decided in its last budget to limit to 5 per cent the growth of the transfer payments made under the Canada Assistance Plan to the provinces of Ontario, British Columbia, and Alberta. For the first time since the beginning of this program 24 years ago, the federal government was limiting its contribution. That means that Ontario stands to lose $90 million in revenues in the next five years, Alberta, $28 million, and British Columbia, $38 million.
In order to justify his decision, the Minister of finance, in the budget Speech he made in 1989, stood up for the clawback of family allowances and old-age benefits, claiming that, and I quote, "the central purpose of social security is to assist those most in need, not to subsidize those with high incomes." But then the measures included in that budget were attacking the poor people in Canada. The governement could use a reminder that

poor people in the provinces of Ontario, British Columbia and Alberta are just as poor as those in the other provinces.
Besides, let us keep in mind that social welfare payments have yet to enable a poor family to rise above the poverty line.
A few days after the last budget was tabled the provinces of British Columbia and Ontario announced their intention of having the courts rule on the propriety of the CAP cut-backs unveiled in the budget. This legal hassle might delay the introduction of this measure until the courts have rendered their decision. Alberta stands four square behind these two provinces. The contesting provinces argue that, under the CAP agreement, arrangements cannot be changed unless a year's notice has been served, and with the consent of the provinces. None of these conditions has been met.
Madam Speaker, in closing I want to say that the Liberal Party is adamantly opposed to Bill C-69 because it amounts to an assault on medicare, post-secondary education and the Canada Assistance Plan. These programs are the basis of Canadian society and as such should be immune to the frustations and meanness of the government.

As the right hon. member for Vancouver Quadra said some time ago, let us hope that hospitals will not be checking our credit cards before they check our pulse. I am afraid that this bill may lead us in that direction.
